Thorough means doing something completely and carefully, making sure nothing is missed, skipped, or left half-done.

When a person or a process is thorough, every single part of the task has been attended to. No corner has been cut. No detail has been overlooked. The job has been done from start to finish with full attention.

Think of it this way: imagine washing dishes. A quick rinse where some food is still stuck is the opposite of thorough. Scrubbing every dish, checking each one, and making sure every spot of grease is gone — that is thorough.

The word "thorough" captures two ideas at the same time:

Completeness — everything has been covered; nothing has been left out.
Care — it was done with attention and diligence, not rushed or done lazily.

A thorough job is not just a complete job. It is a complete job done carefully. Both ingredients must be present. If you finish a task quickly but miss important parts, it is not thorough. If you are careful about the parts you do but skip others, it is still not thorough.

When you say a person is thorough, you mean they have a habit of doing things completely and carefully. They don't cut corners. They check their work. They make sure everything is in order before they stop.

A thorough doctor examines every symptom before giving a diagnosis — not just the obvious ones.

A thorough teacher makes sure every student has understood the lesson before moving on.

A thorough editor reads a document multiple times, checking not just spelling but logic, flow, and facts.

Being thorough is generally seen as a positive quality. It suggests reliability, discipline, and seriousness about one's work.
Used to Describe Actions and Processes

"Thorough" is very commonly used to describe how something was done — an action, a process, or an investigation.

A thorough search means every possible place was looked into.

A thorough cleaning means every surface, corner, and hidden spot was cleaned — nothing was skipped.

A thorough investigation means every clue, witness, and piece of evidence was examined carefully.

A thorough review means a document or plan was read and analysed in full, not just skimmed.

The word signals that the person doing the task gave it their complete attention and left it in a fully finished state.

"Thorough" is a fairly strong word. It doesn't just mean "reasonably careful." It means properly complete — to a degree that leaves no room for doubt that the job was done right. When you call something thorough, you are saying it was done as it should be done — fully, carefully, and without gaps.

Understanding what a word does not mean helps sharpen the picture.

Thorough is not the same as fast. In fact, being thorough often takes more time precisely because you are not rushing.

Thorough is not just detailed. You could be obsessively detailed about one small part of a task while completely ignoring the rest. Thorough means the whole task got that level of care.

Thorough is not the same as strict or harsh. A thorough person can be kind and gentle. Thoroughness is about how completely a task is done, not about personality or attitude.

The clearest opposites of thorough are:

Superficial — only looking at the surface, not going deep or checking properly.
Careless — not paying enough attention to what you are doing.
Hasty — rushing through without proper care.
Incomplete — not finishing every part of the task.

If someone gives a project a superficial look, they have done the opposite of being thorough.

Several words are close in meaning to thorough, but each has a slightly different angle:

Meticulous focuses more on extreme precision and care about tiny details. A meticulous person is very thorough, but the emphasis is on precision rather than completeness.

Exhaustive means something has covered every single possibility — it emphasises breadth (how much ground was covered). An exhaustive list covers everything. Thorough also covers everything, but additionally implies care in how it was done.

Comprehensive means something covers a wide range of things. It is mostly about scope — how much is included. Thorough adds the idea of how carefully it was done.

Careful simply means you paid attention. It lacks the sense of completeness that "thorough" carries.

Thorough is the most balanced of these. It says: this was done completely, and it was done carefully. That is why it is such a useful and widely used word.
How It Fits in a Sentence

The word "thorough" sits before a noun or after a linking verb, just like any standard adjective:

Before a noun: "She carried out a thorough inspection of the building."

After a linking verb: "His research was extremely thorough."

Describing a person: "She is known for being thorough in her work."

Thorough means doing something completely and carefully — covering every part, checking every detail, and leaving nothing out.

If you remember that one sentence, you have captured the full meaning of the word.
